blocks.html: Suppose your teacher asks you to print "I will complete my homework" 100 times. Writing 100 cout statements would be silly. A loop repeats a block of statements as long as a condition is true. Repeating is called iteration, and each repetition is one iteration.
Every loop has four parts:

items.html: Initialisation — give the loop variable a starting value (i = 1 ).
Condition — checked before (or after) each round; the loop continues while it is true (i <= 10 ).
Body — the statements that are repeated.
Update — change the loop variable so that the condition eventually becomes false (i++ ).

blocks.html: The for loop is best when you know how many times to repeat.

items.html: A counter counts how many times something happens: count++ .
An accumulator keeps a running total: sum += x . It must start at 0 (or at 1 for a running product).

blocks.html: A loop inside another loop is a nested loop. For every single round of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely. Nested loops are used for patterns, tables and grids.
In the right triangle, row i prints i stars because the inner loop runs from 1 to i . In the pyramid, row i first prints rows - i spaces to push the stars to the centre.
An infinite loop never ends because its condition never becomes false.

rows: The loop has an empty body; the next line runs only once

blocks.html: If a program gets stuck in an infinite loop, press Ctrl + C to stop it.

Did you know? Your phone's screen is redrawn about 60 times every second by a loop that keeps running as long as the phone is on. Games also run a "game loop": read input, update positions, draw — again and again.
